det_01.label: Origin of the Eurovision dataset
det_01.content: This dataset is the TidyTuesday 2022-05-17 release (week 20) curated from the official Eurovision Song Contest website (eurovision.tv) and Data.World's country-to-country voting archive maintained by datagraver. Tanya Shapiro and Bob Rudis published the scraping code in R using rvest and jsonlite; that code lives in the repo's clean-euro.R. The contestant table covers every act that competed from 1956 through 2022 (with semi-final structure since 2004); the votes table covers every country-to-country point allocation from 1975 to 2019. One row in eurovision.csv is one act in one round of one year; one row in eurovision-votes.csv is one (from_country, to_country, jury-or-televote) point allocation in one round.

det_02.label: What Eurovision is and how voting works
det_02.content: The Eurovision Song Contest is an annual songwriting competition organized by the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), held every May since 1956 (apart from 2020). Each participating broadcaster sends one original song of three minutes or less, performed live by a singer or group of up to six. Each country awards two ranked sets of points (1-8, 10, and 12) - one from a national jury of music professionals and one from public televoting - to its favorite songs in the grand final; it cannot vote for itself. Semi-finals were introduced in 2004 (and split into two semis from 2008). The current 50/50 jury+televote split was introduced in 2009 specifically because broadcasters worried that pure televoting was being captured by Eastern-bloc voting alliances. As of 2022, 52 countries had taken part at least once, and Australia has competed since 2015 despite not being in Europe.

det_03.label: Bloc voting and diaspora effects
det_03.content: Eurovision's voting patterns are notoriously non-random. Researchers at Maynooth University, Lancaster (Derek Gatherer's JASSS simulation), and others have shown that countries cluster into self-supporting blocs - Nordic, ex-Yugoslav, former-Soviet, Baltic, and a Greek-Cypriot pair - that systematically award each other higher points than chance would predict. Diaspora effects compound this: Greece and Turkey reliably draw heavy points from Germany; Poland and Lithuania from the UK; ex-Yugoslav states from each other. The most extreme pair is Greece-Cyprus: between 1997 and 2013, the two countries awarded each other 12 points (the maximum) in essentially every grand final where both competed; Cyprus has given Greece 12 points in 27 of 32 final voting opportunities through 2024. The EBU introduced the 2009 jury reform explicitly to dilute these televote-driven blocs.

det_04.label: 2022: a vote for Ukraine, not just for Stefania
det_04.content: Eurovision 2022 was held in Turin, Italy, less than three months after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Ukrainian entry, Kalush Orchestra's folk-rap hybrid 'Stefania', was a mid-pack jury favorite (4th by jury) but won the public televote by an enormous margin - 439 televote points to Spain's 228 and the UK's 183, contributing to a final tally of 631 points, the second-highest ever. Frontman Oleh Psiuk closed the performance with a plea to free the Ukrainian fighters trapped under the Azovstal steel plant in Mariupol; the EBU declined to penalize the band, calling the comments humanitarian. The song was originally written for Psiuk's mother before the war but reframed as a patriotic anthem after February 24. The 2022 result is the cleanest modern example of geopolitical empathy showing up in televote scores - the kind of pattern the 50/50 jury reform was meant to mute, and didn't.

det_05.label: Ireland and Sweden: the dynasty era
det_05.content: Ireland holds the record (jointly with Sweden, who tied it in 2023) for most Eurovision wins, with seven, but the Irish wins are concentrated in a single five-year run nobody has matched: 1992 (Linda Martin), 1993 (Niamh Kavanagh) and 1994 (Paul Harrington and Charlie McGettigan) - three consecutive wins, the only such streak in the contest's history - plus 1996 (Eimear Quinn). Add Dana (1970), Johnny Logan (1980, 1987) and Ireland produces seven trophies in 26 years. Sweden's seven cluster differently: ABBA's 1974 'Waterloo' put the contest on the global pop map and remains the song most often voted Eurovision's all-time best. Loreen, who won in 2012 and 2023, is the only artist to win twice as a soloist.

det_06.label: The 2003 nul-points and the jury-televote pendulum
det_06.content: In 2003, the UK's Jemini scored zero points - the first time the United Kingdom had ever finished bottom of Eurovision. The result was widely attributed to a combination of an off-key live performance (the duo's earpieces failed) and European hostility toward the UK over its participation in the Iraq invasion two months earlier. Sir Terry Wogan blamed the latter. The 2003 contest used a pure-televote system, which had been reinstated in 2002 after a jury-cheating scandal. Six years later, the EBU swung the pendulum back to the 50/50 jury+televote split that still defines the contest, explicitly to prevent televote sweeps and political voting. The 2003 nul-points is therefore a useful before-and-after marker: in the data, jury and televote scores from the same country can diverge wildly, and entries can win the public while losing the jury (Ukraine 2022, Italy 2021) or vice versa.

det_07.label: Iconic moments: ABBA, Lordi, Conchita
det_07.content: Three Eurovision wins are routinely cited as the moments that defined the contest's cultural meaning beyond Europe. ABBA's 'Waterloo' for Sweden in 1974 - silver platform boots, 24 points, the first global pop hit launched by Eurovision - was voted the best song in contest history at the 2005 50th-anniversary special. Finland's Lordi won in 2006 with 'Hard Rock Hallelujah', a heavy-metal screamo anthem performed in monster prosthetics; their 292 points were a record at the time. Austria's Conchita Wurst won in 2014 with 'Rise Like a Phoenix', a Bond-style power ballad performed by drag artist Tom Neuwirth in a beard - a result widely framed as a triumph for LGBTQ+ visibility, especially against Russian and Belarusian backlash. These three wins anchor the dataset's emotional range: pop polish, novelty maximalism, and identity-politics ballad. Each has an official Eurovision-channel video on YouTube that can be embedded.

det_08.label: Benchmark: chance baseline for 12-point exchanges
det_08.content: When researchers test for bloc voting, the relevant baseline is: 'how often would two countries award each other the maximum if they were voting at random over their available repertoires?' In a final with N qualified countries, a country distributes 10 ranked scores (1-8, 10, 12) over up to N-1 others, so the chance of awarding any specific other country exactly 12 points is 1/(N-1). For a 26-country final that is 3.85% per direction. The chance of a mutual exchange in any given year is therefore on the order of 0.15% by chance alone. Greece-Cyprus exchanged 12 points in 17 of 17 finals between 1997 and 2013 in which both competed - a probability under random voting of roughly 1.5e-26. This is the benchmark Designer can compare actual reciprocity rates to.

det_09.label: Scope suggestions for the analyst
det_09.content: The data has three clean angles worth deep analysis: (1) Win counts and consistency by country - who actually wins, how often, and which countries are perennial finalists vs. perennial bottom-finishers. (2) Bloc-voting evidence in eurovision-votes.csv - quantify reciprocal 12-point exchanges, mean points awarded to bloc neighbors vs. non-neighbors, and whether the post-2009 jury reform actually reduced bloc voting (split jury vs televote rows). (3) Jury-vs-televote divergence in 2016-2019 (when split scores are recorded) - which entries split the audience hardest. The analyst should NOT treat 2020 as missing data - the contest was cancelled. Likewise, the 1996 'audio-only' entry round is an asterisk in pre-2004 entries. Finally, country names changed over the period (Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro, etc.) - treat as one row per recorded name and flag splits.
